nameStory: The name 'blood lichen' comes from the reddish pigments that give this lichen family their characteristic bloody appearance. When crushed or scratched, many species in this group release red or orange compounds that look remarkably like drops of blood on the bark.
description: This blood lichen forms thin, crusty patches that spread across tree bark like a rough, painted coating. The thallus (lichen body) appears grayish-white to pale greenish when dry, but may show subtle reddish tones in certain lighting or when damaged. It typically grows in irregular patches a few inches across, though older specimens can cover larger areas of bark.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating (crustose) that's tightly bonded to bark and impossible to peel off without damaging

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Appears pale gray to whitish when dry, sometimes with a subtle greenish tint when moist, and may show reddish staining when scratched

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and granular to the touch, like fine sandpaper, with an uneven, slightly bumpy surface

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like maple and beech

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Produces small, dark brown to blackish disc-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that look like tiny buttons pressed into the surface

habitat: This rare lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees in mature forests throughout New England, showing a preference for areas with clean air and stable moisture conditions. It's most often found on trees with relatively smooth bark like maples, beeches, and birches in undisturbed woodland settings.

seasonality.spring: Best observed when spring rains darken the bark and make the lichen's subtle colors more visible. The contrast between wet bark and the lighter lichen patches is most pronounced now.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen appears at its palest and most cryptic against sun-bleached bark. Look for it in shaded areas where moisture lingers longer.
seasonality.fall: Autumn's increased humidity brings out any greenish tints in the lichen, and falling leaves may reveal previously hidden patches on tree trunks.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice can make the lichen stand out dramatically against dark, wet bark. This is often the easiest season to spot the subtle color differences that distinguish it from similar species.

funFact: Despite being called 'blood lichen,' the red pigments in this group aren't just for show—they actually help protect the lichen from harmful UV radiation, working like a natural sunscreen that can last for decades.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pale, crusty lichens on bark, but the potential for reddish staining when damaged and its preference for smooth-barked deciduous trees help distinguish it. Remember: if it bleeds red when scratched, you're likely looking at a blood lichen.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so any potential sighting should be documented carefully and verified by experts. The scientific name 'sanguinarioides' means 'resembling sanguinarius,' referring to its similarity to the more common Bloody-heart Lichen.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Bloody-heart Lichen, this species tends to be paler overall and may have less obvious red pigmentation. The differences are quite subtle and often require chemical testing or microscopic examination to confirm, making field identification challenging even for experts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Mycoblastus sanguinarioides is extremely similar and also bleeds red when scratched, making them very difficult to tell apart in the field.
